title: Salman Khan's Maatrubhumi Clears Key Hurdle as Revised Cut Recasts China Ties
excerpt: The war drama once titled Battle of Galwan has a government no-objection certificate after months in limbo — but the version audiences will see reportedly frames India-China relations in a far softer light.
body:
• The I&B Ministry has issued a No Objection Certificate for Maatrubhumi, Salman Khan's war drama once titled Battle of Galwan, after the makers submitted a substantially revised cut — reportedly issued last week, according to Bollywood Hungama's exclusive report.
  • The delay stemmed from Ministry of Defence reservations over the film's portrayal of China as India-China ties improved; the new version reportedly frames the relationship between the two countries in a positive light.
  • Salman Khan is said to be eyeing a November 13 theatrical release, but the censor process is still pending — the makers must still submit the film to the CBFC before any date can be confirmed.

Salman Khan's war drama Maatrubhumi has finally cleared a decisive government hurdle, moving the long-delayed film a significant step closer to theaters. According to an exclusive report in Bollywood Hungama, officials of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting are satisfied with the revised version of the film submitted by the makers and issued a No Objection Certificate (NOC) last week — effectively green-lighting it for public consumption.

"The officials of the I&B Ministry are now satisfied with the new version of Maatrubhumi submitted by the makers. Hence, they gave an NOC to the war saga last week. This means that the film can now be made available for public consumption," a source told Bollywood Hungama. The film's producers have not yet officially confirmed the development.

A war film stalled by diplomacy

The road to this clearance has been anything but smooth. The film was announced as Battle of Galwan — a direct reference to the 2020 military clash between Indian and Chinese troops in the Galwan Valley — and was rechristened Maatrubhumi earlier this year. Directed by Apoorva Lakhia and co-starring Chitrangda Singh, the project was held up after the Ministry of Defence raised reservations about its content and its references to China, at a time when relations between the two countries were improving.

The objections forced a lengthy rethink. In April, Mid-Day reported that direct references to China were being removed and the revised narrative was being shaped to carry a message of peace rather than glorify war. The makers are said to have undertaken roughly 40 days of reshoots — at one point even considering a Chinese-language song — to bring the film in line with the government's sensitivities.

What changed in the new cut

The most striking part of the reported overhaul is the tonal shift. "The new version of Maatrubhumi is highly altered compared to the original version," the source told Bollywood Hungama. "Moreover, it now also talks about the relationship between India and China in a positive light."

That is a remarkable evolution for a project that began life as a battle-of-Galwan war saga. War cinema traditionally leans on clear dramatic divisions — hero and adversary — but Maatrubhumi's journey shows how closely Bollywood's nationalism films now track real-world diplomacy. A country can be the adversary in one historical moment and an essential diplomatic partner in another, and a film dealing with recent conflict has to negotiate between historical memory and present-day realities.

A Diwali-season release race

With the I&B hurdle cleared, attention has turned to the calendar. Salman Khan is reportedly eyeing November 13 for release — just after Diwali, a period he believes will keep audiences in a celebratory mood. But one major gate remains: the Central Board of Film Certification. The makers will submit the film to the CBFC shortly, and if certification comes through this month, the November date could hold.

The film's diaspora release will be one to watch. A post-Diwali Salman Khan war drama would be among the biggest Hindi releases of the year in overseas markets, where war films with patriotic themes routinely pull strong numbers in the US, UK, and Gulf. For North American exhibitors planning their November Indian-film slate, the next ten days — when a clearer picture is expected to emerge — will determine whether Maatrubhumi anchors the month.

What's next

The immediate question is the censor process. If the CBFC passes the revised cut without cuts of its own, November 13 is in play; if the board wants changes, the film could slip further. Either way, Maatrubhumi has become an unlikely case study in how geopolitics now shapes Bollywood's biggest films — from title to soundtrack to story — before a single ticket is sold. https://youtube.com/watch?v=WWthtnGbxUM
